metric.semantic_determinacy.basis: all 44 fixed probes assigned to this shard (single-language, single-probe-group worker)
limitations: This is a single-shard, single-worker measurement covering only Go; cross-language comparability and the 'common basis' requirement of the interaction_with_quality_metrics section must be reconciled by the runner once all language shards for this metric are merged.

B_i counts were assigned by expert analysis of the Go language specification and standard library documentation from this packet's embedded probe definitions; no external tool execution, compiler run, or live documentation fetch was performed (packet-only mode, no network/tools). No fragment source text was produced or built under the frozen recipe by this worker; V1 (build-and-match) evidence for the underlying fragments must come from whichever worker authors and compiles the Go fragments for capability coverage.

The linear-cap normalization formula (cap at log2(8)=3) is this worker's own documented convention for presenting a 0-100 number; it is not asserted to be the run's canonical cross-language normalization curve.
metric.semantic_determinacy.method: Spec 6.1.3.B: for each probe, count B_i = number of materially different semantic interpretations compatible with the local surface form alone (call-site/ordinary form; explicit reference forms measured separately per probe design). Record raw B_i and log2(B_i); raw metric value = mean(log2(B_i)) over the 44 probes. Lower is better.
metric.semantic_determinacy.normalization_note: This worker computes and reports the raw mean(log2(B_i)) and additionally publishes a normalized 0-100 score using the documented linear-cap formula normalized = 100 * clamp(1 - raw/3, 0, 1), where 3 = log2(8) is used as a practical worst-case branching bound observed across probe families in this universe (no probe assigned B_i > 4 for Go). This cap is a worker-level documented choice, not a cross-language-calibrated constant; if the runner's aggregation defines a different fixed normalization curve for this metric, the raw per-probe table below is sufficient to recompute the normalized score under that curve without re-measurement.

per_probe.rationale: `const n = 7; return n` — const binding is unambiguously an immutable value, no storage; single interpretation.
`var counter int64 = 0` (mutable) vs `const LIMIT int64 = 100` (immutable) — Go's var/const keywords make mutability unambiguous from the declaration form alone.
`var v int32` is always zero-initialized in Go (spec-guaranteed); the two-way branch with definite assignment on both paths leaves no ambiguity about v's value or definedness.
Go has no way to request genuinely uninitialized bulk storage; the substituted always-zero-initialized `[16]byte` array leaves no interpretation ambiguity (P-a substitution, but determinate).
`x++` — in-place, single well-defined wraparound-on-overflow semantics for signed ints in Go.
`xs[1] = 42` on a slice — deterministic in-place element write to the shared backing array.
`port := &slot; *port = 9` — explicit pointer/dereference, single interpretation.

Go has no read-only slice view type; re-slicing (`window := xs[:]`) shares the backing array but does not statically prevent writes through window, so a reader cannot locally determine from the form alone whether write-through is intended to be forbidden or merely unused; two materially different readings (view-as-read-only convention vs. fully writable alias) remain.
`first == second` on pointer-typed values after routing through a container round trip is Go's unambiguous reference-identity comparison.

Bare call site `f(x)` alone (excluding f's declaration) leaves f's parameter type unknown: it could be declared as the slice type itself (shared backing array; callee can write elements, cannot resize-visibly), a pointer to slice, an interface value, or a value type requiring conversion — at least 4 materially distinct aliasing/mutation outcomes remain compatible with the call-site syntax alone, matching the frozen outcome set in the probe's scoring note.
`put(cell *int32)` / `put(&cell)` — explicit pointer parameter and address-of at the call site make writable-alias passing unambiguous.
`neg := func(a int32) int32 { return k - a }` — closures capture by reference to the enclosing variable in a single well-defined way in Go.
Returning `xs[1]` (an int32) is a value-copy return; Go has no reference-return ambiguity for non-pointer element types.
Named multiple return values `(int32, int32)` and `q, r := divmod2(a, b)` are Go's single normal multi-result mechanism.
`r := a*b + c` — standard precedence and fixed-width signed int arithmetic, single interpretation.
`q := a / b; m := a % b; d := float64(a) / float64(b)` — explicit conversions required for float division, truncating integer division and sign-following remainder are spec-fixed.
Go signed integer overflow is spec-defined two's-complement wraparound; `o := m + 1` has one deterministic outcome (rung iv, no higher rung available in the standard library).
Explicit `if b == 0 { q = 0 } else { q = a / b }` guard (rung ii, no checked-division standard op exists) is fully determinate at the site.
`s1 == s2` on Go's built-in string type is always content comparison; no user-defined/dynamic dispatch is possible for the built-in type.
`sort.Slice(xs, func(i,j int) bool { return xs[i] > xs[j] })` explicitly supplies the descending comparator and is documented to sort in place.
`small := int32(big)` — Go's explicit narrowing conversion truncates deterministically (rung ii/iii, no checked-conversion standard op exists).
`sum := float64(i) + d` — Go requires an explicit conversion for mixed-type arithmetic; no implicit promotion exists, so the site is fully determinate.
`e := xs[i]` — out-of-range index panics; this is Go's single defined outcome for the ordinary indexed-read form.
`part := xs[1:4]` — slicing is spec-guaranteed to share the backing array (no copy); single interpretation.

Go has no Option type; the substituted sentinel (nil pointer, or a bool-flag struct) leaves two plausible standard idioms (pointer-based vs comma-ok-style struct) compatible with the local form (P-a substitution).

No standard optional-chaining operation exists in Go; the substituted explicit conditional could be written as an `if ptr != nil` guard or a helper-function call, leaving two materially different local readings of how absence short-circuits (P-a substitution).
`n, err := strconv.Atoi(s); if err != nil { return 0, err }; return n*2, nil` — Go's multi-value error return and explicit propagation are unambiguous from the declaration and body.
`n, err := strconv.Atoi(s); if err != nil { n = 0 }` — explicit local handling with a single deterministic fallback path.

Go has no closed sum type; substituting an interface with two implementing structs leaves genuine ambiguity at the local declaration about whether the alternative set is meant to be closed or is only conventionally treated as such (P-a substitution).

A type-switch without a default case is not statically checked for exhaustiveness in Go; the local form leaves two readings for what happens on an unhandled type (silent fallthrough vs. runtime panic depend on switch construction, not visible locally).
Interfaces are structurally and openly implementable from any package in Go; a `Tri` type in a separate package implementing `area()` is unambiguous.
Go 1.18+ generic function `func head[T any](xs []T) T { return xs[0] }` has a statically recoverable result type T; single interpretation.
`func max_of[T constraints.Ordered](a, b T) T` — the declaration-site constraint is explicit and checked at declaration.
`items []Named` holding two concrete types dispatched via interface method call is Go's single standard runtime-dispatch idiom.
`xs := []int32{1,2,3}` then a `for range` accumulation loop (no stdlib sum/fold exists) is the single R10-selected form.

`mp := map[string]int32{"a":1}`; `for range` (iteration order intentionally unspecified but this does not create ambiguity in the summed *value*, since summation is order-independent); `miss, ok := mp["b"]` comma-ok lookup with explicit substitution of 0 is fully determinate for the miss case.
`defer f.Close()` immediately after a successful `os.Open` guarantees release on every exit path including the read-failure path; single interpretation.

Go has no deterministic destructor; achieving a truly block-scoped (not function-scoped) cleanup point requires wrapping the block in an anonymous function literal so `defer` fires at that literal's return — the plain `defer` form and the wrapped-literal form are both locally plausible substitutes for the required 'block ends' semantics (P-a substitution), leaving two readings of exactly when cleanup fires.
`import "fmt"; fmt.Println("x")` — single standard idiom, unambiguous provenance of Println.
Go's capitalization-based export rule (`PubAdd` exported, `secret` unexported) is a single, purely local, syntactically visible convention with compiler-enforced boundary.
`go func(){...}()` twice plus `sync.WaitGroup.Wait()` (or channel receive) is Go's single standard concurrency-join idiom.
`sync/atomic.AddInt64` or a `sync.Mutex`-guarded increment is Go's single standard documented race-free discipline for this pattern.
`import "C"; C.abs(C.int(-3))` via cgo is Go's single built-in FFI mechanism for calling a C function.
`//export add2` cgo directive above a Go function is the single built-in mechanism for exporting a C-ABI symbol from Go.
